unit-alg-t2-02.title: Topic 2 · 2-2 Standard Form of a Quadratic Function
unit-alg-t2-02.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 2-2: Standard Form of a Quadratic Function

cards.def:
**y = ax² + bx + c, where a, b, and c are real numbers and a ≠ 0.**
• Unlike vertex form, the vertex is not read directly — it has to be found.
• c is the one piece of vertex form-style information standard form hands you for free.
cards.hint: Standard form is what you get when you expand vertex form out.

cards.def:
**h = −b ⁄ 2a.**
• This comes from converting vertex form to standard form and matching up the b term.
• Once you have h, substitute it back into the original equation to get k.
cards.hint: Half of b, over a, with the sign flipped.

cards.def:
**The y-intercept is always (0, c).**
• Substituting x = 0 into y = ax² + bx + c leaves only c.
• It's the one piece of information standard form gives you instantly, with no computation.
cards.hint: Set x to 0 in your head — everything but c disappears.

cards.term: Axis of symmetry from standard form
cards.def:
**x = −b ⁄ 2a — the same formula as the vertex's x-coordinate, because they're the same line.**
• The axis of symmetry always passes through the vertex.
• Any point on the graph has a mirror point the same distance on the other side of this line.
cards.hint: Same formula you just used for h — it's not a coincidence.

cards.def:
**Plot the vertex, plot the y-intercept, then reflect the y-intercept across the axis of symmetry for a third point.**
• Three points are enough to sketch an accurate parabola.
• The reflected point is the same distance from the axis as the y-intercept, on the other side.
cards.hint: Two points from the equation, one for free by symmetry.

cards.term: Maximum vs. minimum from standard form
cards.def:
**a > 0 means the vertex is a minimum; a < 0 means it's a maximum.**
• Same rule as vertex form — only the sign of a decides this.
• The maximum or minimum VALUE is k, the vertex's y-coordinate.
cards.hint: Positive a: valley (minimum). Negative a: hill (maximum).

cards.term: Writing standard form from three points
cards.def:
**Substitute each point's x and y into y = ax² + bx + c to build three equations, then solve the system for a, b, and c.**
• Three unknowns need three equations — that's why three points are required.
• Elimination or substitution both work to solve the system.
cards.hint: Three points, three unknowns, one system — the same idea as solving any linear system, just with quadratic-looking equations.

cards.def:
**In an application, the vertex is usually the best or worst outcome the model predicts — a maximum profit, a peak height, a minimum cost.**
• The x-coordinate of the vertex tells you WHEN or AT WHAT INPUT that outcome happens.
• The y-coordinate tells you WHAT that best or worst value actually is.
cards.hint: Two questions, one point: "at what input" and "what's the result" both live in the vertex.
Compute h first, then plug it back in for k — two separate steps, not one formula.
Negative a means this vertex is a maximum, not a minimum.

cards.term: Comparing standard form and vertex form
cards.def:
**Standard form is easier to write down from data; vertex form is easier to read the vertex from.**
• A y-intercept is instant in standard form, but takes a substitution in vertex form.
• A vertex is instant in vertex form, but takes the h = −b/2a formula in standard form.
cards.hint: Each form makes ONE thing easy and hides another — that's the whole reason both exist.

cards.term: Solving a system of three equations
cards.def:
**Eliminate one variable at a time, the same way you solve a linear system — just with three unknowns instead of two.**
• Subtract pairs of equations to cancel c first, since it appears un-multiplied in every equation.
• That leaves two equations in a and b, which is a system you already know how to solve.
cards.hint: Cancel c first — it's the only variable with no coefficient attached in every equation.

questions.q: In standard form y = ax² + bx + c, what point is the y-intercept?
questions.hint: Substitute x = 0 and see what's left.
steps: The y-intercept happens where x = 0.
Substitute x = 0 into y = ax² + bx + c: y = a(0)² + b(0) + c.
Every term but c disappears, so the y-intercept is (0, c).

ex.main: **(0, c).** This is the one piece of information standard form hands you with zero computation.

questions.q: What formula gives the x-coordinate of the vertex of y = ax² + bx + c?
questions.hint: There's a minus sign in front, and it's b over 2a.
steps: The x-coordinate of the vertex comes from converting standard form back to vertex form.
That conversion produces the formula h = −b/(2a).
So h = −b/(2a) — not b/(2a), and not built from c.

ex.main: **h = −b/(2a).** Missing the negative sign is the single most common error with this formula.

questions.q: What is the y-intercept of y = 7x² − 3x + 20?
questions.hint: It's just c, as a point.
steps: The y-intercept of any standard-form quadratic is (0, c).
Here c = 20.
So the y-intercept is (0, 20).

ex.main: **(0, 20).** No computation needed — c IS the y-intercept's y-value.

questions.q: What is the vertex of y = x² − 8x + 15?
questions.hint: Find h with the formula first, then substitute back to find k.
steps: Substitute h = 4 back into the equation: (4)² − 8(4) + 15 = 16 − 32 + 15.
That simplifies to −1, so the vertex is (4, −1).

ex.main: **(4, −1).** Two separate steps: the formula gives h, then substitution gives k — there's no formula that hands you both at once.

questions.q: What is the vertex of y = −2x² + 12x − 7?
questions.hint: Watch the sign of a in the denominator.
steps: Substitute h = 3 back in: −2(3)² + 12(3) − 7 = −18 + 36 − 7.
That simplifies to 11, so the vertex is (3, 11).

ex.main: **(3, 11).** With a negative a in the denominator, two negatives — the formula's minus sign and a's own sign — cancel to a positive h.

questions.q: Does y = 3x² − 6x + 2 have a maximum or a minimum, and what is its value?
questions.hint: Check the sign of a first to know which kind it is.
steps: a = 3 is positive, so the vertex is a minimum, not a maximum.
Substitute back: 3(1)² − 6(1) + 2 = 3 − 6 + 2 = −1. The minimum value is −1.

ex.main: **Minimum, at y = −1.** Positive a rules out "maximum" before you even compute the vertex.

questions.q: Does y = −x² + 10x − 13 have a maximum or a minimum, and what is its value?
questions.hint: Negative a settles the maximum-or-minimum question immediately.
steps: a = −1 is negative, so the vertex is a maximum.
Substitute back: −(5)² + 10(5) − 13 = −25 + 50 − 13 = 12. The maximum value is 12.

ex.main: **Maximum, at y = 12.**

questions.q: A company's profit, in dollars, from selling x units is y = −5x² + 300x − 2000. How many units should they sell to maximize profit, and what is that maximum profit?
questions.hint: The vertex's x-value answers "how many units"; its y-value answers "how much profit".
steps: That simplifies to 2500. So 30 units gives a maximum profit of $2,500.

ex.main: **30 units, for $2,500.** The vertex's x tells you the input that produces the best outcome; its y tells you what that outcome actually is — two different questions, one point.

questions.q: A parabola passes through (−1, 6), (1, 0), and (3, 10). What is its equation in standard form?
questions.hint: Substitute each point to build three equations, then solve for a, b, and c.
steps: Substitute each point into y = ax² + bx + c: from (−1, 6): a − b + c = 6. From (1, 0): a + b + c = 0. From (3, 10): 9a + 3b + c = 10.
Subtract the first two equations to eliminate c: (a + b + c) − (a − b + c) = 0 − 6, giving 2b = −6, so b = −3.
Substitute b = −3 back into a + b + c = 0 and 9a + 3b + c = 10, and solve the remaining system: a = 2, c = 1. The equation is y = 2x² − 3x + 1.

ex.main: **y = 2x² − 3x + 1.** Three points, three unknowns — exactly enough information and no more.

questions.q: A parabola passes through (0, 2), (2, 6), and (5, −3). What is its equation in standard form?
questions.hint: One of the points has x = 0 — that shortcuts finding c.
steps: Since (0, 2) is on the parabola, c = 2 immediately — no elimination needed for that part.
Substitute the other two points into y = ax² + bx + 2: from (2, 6): 4a + 2b + 2 = 6, so 4a + 2b = 4. From (5, −3): 25a + 5b + 2 = −3, so 25a + 5b = −5.
Solve the two-equation system: from 4a + 2b = 4, b = 2 − 2a. Substitute into 25a + 5(2 − 2a) = −5: 25a + 10 − 10a = −5, so 15a = −15, a = −1, and b = 2 − 2(−1) = 4. The equation is y = −x² + 4x + 2.

ex.main: **y = −x² + 4x + 2.** A point with x = 0 is worth spotting first — it gives you c for free and turns a three-variable system into a two-variable one.

questions.q: What is the axis of symmetry of y = 4x² + 8x − 3?
questions.hint: Same formula as the vertex's x-coordinate.
steps: The axis of symmetry is x = −b/(2a).
So the axis of symmetry is x = −1.

ex.main: **x = −1.** Vertex's x-coordinate and axis of symmetry are the same formula because the axis of symmetry always runs through the vertex.

questions.q: A parabola has y-intercept (0, 8) and axis of symmetry x = 2. Which point must also be on the graph?
questions.hint: Reflect the y-intercept across the axis of symmetry.
steps: The y-intercept (0, 8) is 2 units to the left of the axis of symmetry, x = 2.
By symmetry, there's a matching point 2 units to the RIGHT of the axis, at the same height.
2 units right of x = 2 is x = 4, so the matching point is (4, 8).

ex.main: **(4, 8).** Reflecting the y-intercept across the axis of symmetry is a free third point — no extra equation needed.

questions.q: Devin says the vertex of any quadratic function can be read directly from its standard form, the same way it can from vertex form. Is Devin correct?
opts: No — standard form requires computing h = −b/(2a) first, then substituting for k
Yes — h is always a, and k is always c
No — standard form never reveals the vertex, no matter what you compute
Yes — the vertex is always (b, c) in standard form
questions.hint: Compare what each form hands you for free.
steps: Vertex form is built so the vertex (h, k) can be read straight off the equation with no computation.
Standard form does not have this property — the vertex has to be computed using h = −b/(2a), then k found by substitution.
So Devin is incorrect: standard form requires computation the vertex form doesn't.

ex.main: **No — it takes computing h = −b/(2a) first, then substituting for k.** That extra work is the whole trade-off standard form makes for being easier to build from raw data.

questions.q: For y = 6x² − 5x + 9, what is the value of c?
questions.hint: c is the constant term at the end.
steps: In standard form y = ax² + bx + c, c is whichever term has no x attached to it.
In y = 6x² − 5x + 9, that term is 9.
So c = 9.

ex.main: **9.** c is just the constant sitting at the end of the equation — no computation required.

questions.q: A ball's height is modeled by y = −16x² + 48x + 5, where x is time in seconds. A second ball is modeled by y = −16x² + 64x + 2. Which ball reaches a greater maximum height?
opts: They reach the same maximum height
There isn't enough information to tell
questions.hint: Find each vertex's y-value and compare them.
steps: 66 is greater than 41, so the second ball reaches a greater maximum height.

ex.main: **The second ball, reaching 66 ft against the first ball's 41 ft.** Comparing two models means finding both vertices, not just glancing at the coefficients.

questions.q: Amos says the y-intercept of a quadratic function always tells you its maximum value. What is his error?
opts: The y-intercept is the height at x = 0, not necessarily the highest or lowest point
The y-intercept is always the minimum, never the maximum
The y-intercept only applies when a is negative
There is no error — Amos is correct
questions.hint: Compare what x = 0 means versus what the vertex means.
steps: The y-intercept is simply the value of the function when x = 0 — nothing more.
The maximum or minimum value is the y-coordinate of the VERTEX, which is usually at a different x-value entirely.
So Amos's error is treating the y-intercept as if it were automatically the vertex, when it usually isn't.

ex.main: **The y-intercept is just the height at x = 0 — it's the vertex's y-value that gives the actual maximum or minimum.**

questions.q: How many known points are required to write the standard-form equation of a parabola from scratch?
questions.hint: Count the unknowns in y = ax² + bx + c.
steps: Standard form has three unknown coefficients: a, b, and c.
Each known point gives one equation relating those three unknowns.
Three unknowns need three independent equations to solve, so three points are required.

ex.main: **Three.** One equation per unknown — a, b, and c — is what makes the system solvable exactly.

questions.q: A rocket's height is modeled by y = −5x² + 40x, where x is time in seconds. What is the rocket's height at launch (x = 0), and what does that tell you about c in this equation?
opts: 0 ft, which matches c = 0 in the equation
There's no way to know without graphing
questions.hint: This equation has no constant term written — what does that mean for c?
steps: The height at launch is the height when x = 0: y = −5(0)² + 40(0) = 0.
The y-intercept of this equation is (0, c), and no constant term is written, meaning c = 0.
Both agree: the rocket starts at a height of 0 ft, matching c = 0.

ex.main: **0 ft, matching c = 0.** A missing constant term in standard form always means c = 0, and this rocket model makes sense that way — it launches from the ground.

questions.q: Which of these equations is written in standard form?
questions.hint: Standard form is fully expanded — no parentheses left.
steps: Standard form has the shape y = ax² + bx + c, with everything already expanded — no factors or squared binomials left.
y = 3(x − 1)² + 4 is vertex form. y = (x − 3)(x + 2) and y = −4(x + 5)² both still have unexpanded factors.
Only y = 5x² − 2x + 9 is fully expanded into standard form.

ex.main: **y = 5x² − 2x + 9.** It's the only option with no parentheses left to expand.

questions.q: A parabola opens downward, has axis of symmetry x = −2, and passes through (0, −5) and (−4, −5). What can you conclude about its vertex without solving for a, b, and c?
opts: Its x-coordinate is −2, and its y-coordinate is greater than −5
Its x-coordinate is −5, and its y-coordinate is −2
Its x-coordinate is −2, and its y-coordinate is less than −5
Nothing can be concluded without the full equation
questions.hint: The axis of symmetry gives h directly. The direction it opens tells you how k compares to nearby points.
steps: The axis of symmetry is always x = h, so the vertex's x-coordinate is −2 — no equation needed.
(0, −5) and (−4, −5) are symmetric across x = −2, confirming that axis, and both sit ON the parabola.
Since the parabola opens downward, its vertex is the highest point on the graph — so its y-coordinate must be greater than −5, the height of those two points.

ex.main: **x-coordinate −2, y-coordinate greater than −5.** The axis of symmetry and the opening direction both come free, without any algebra — reading the graph's shape is its own kind of solving.
